projects.name: Hybrid VQC Weather Forecasting with FPGA Inference
projects.blurb: 7-qubit variational circuit for 24-day temperature forecasting, with a custom kernel on an AMD Alveo FPGA for low-latency edge inference.
projects.abstract: A hybrid quantum-classical model that forecasts temperature 24 days ahead from daily NCMRWF reanalysis data, using a 7-qubit variational quantum circuit (50 parameters) with StronglyEntanglingLayers. For low-latency inference, the frozen model runs on a custom AMD Alveo U55C FPGA kernel built with HLS.
projects.role: Co-author (with first author N. Khan), IEEE TQCEBT 2026.

sections.p: 24-day-ahead temperature forecasting is hard: atmospheric dynamics are nonlinear and labelled data is limited. The question was whether a compact variational quantum circuit, trained on daily NCMRWF reanalysis data, could learn useful long-range patterns, and whether its inference could run fast enough for edge use.

The model is a 7-qubit variational quantum circuit with 50 trainable parameters, using angle encoding to map meteorological variables onto the qubits and two StronglyEntanglingLayers as the ansatz. It was trained, validated and tested in PennyLane on a CPU-based quantum simulator, reaching a test RMSE of 3.01 K and R² of 0.801.

For low-latency edge inference, the frozen model runs on a custom Vitis HLS kernel on an AMD Alveo U55C FPGA; the kernel exchanges batches of input features, pre-trained weights and expectation values with the host over HBM.
A hybrid VQC forecaster with low-latency FPGA inference for edge use. Published at IEEE TQCEBT 2026.

projects.paper: Hybrid variational quantum circuits based temperature forecasting with low-latency FPGA inference
layman: Weather forecasting means predicting the future from today's measurements. This project asked whether a small quantum circuit could learn temperature patterns 24 days ahead from daily reanalysis records (NCMRWF data), and whether the trained model could answer quickly enough to run on a small device at the edge.

A variational quantum circuit works like a tunable recipe. Weather measurements are written into the rotation angles of 7 qubits, a fixed pattern of entangling gates mixes them, and 50 adjustable settings are tuned during training until the circuit's measured outputs match the recorded temperatures.

Once trained, the recipe is frozen. The same calculation was then written as a custom circuit for an FPGA, a chip whose wiring can be programmed for one job, so that forecasts come back with low delay.

projects.name: Quantum Image Representation Neural Networks
projects.blurb: Quantum neural networks for binary image classification built on four quantum image encodings: NASS, QBIR, FTQR and FRQCI.
projects.abstract: A controlled comparison of four quantum image representations (NASS, QBIR, FTQR, FRQCI) inside one variational quantum neural network framework for image classification on near-term (NISQ) devices, tested on binary MNIST (0 vs 1) and a three-class FashionMNIST subset at resolutions from 2×2 to 16×16, under both noiseless simulation and a calibrated noise model of the IBM Heron r3 processor. Two reference models, a quanvolutional network (QCNN) and a hybrid CNN–QNN (HCQNN), place the encodings against established baselines.
projects.role: I conceived this study: the question of how the choice of quantum image encoding shapes the trainability, noise robustness and cost of variational QNNs. I designed the experimental protocol, selected and implemented the four encodings (NASS, QBIR, FTQR, FRQCI) in a single QNN framework, and carried out the comparative analysis, the visualisations and the organisation of results. During revision, in response to referee and editor feedback from The Journal of Supercomputing, I also carried out the state-of-the-art comparison, the gradient (trainability) analysis and the mathematical modelling.

sections.p: Quantum image classification depends heavily on how classical pixel data is encoded into quantum states, but encodings are often chosen by convention rather than by measured trade-off.

Four quantum image representations — Normal Arbitrary Superposition State (NASS), Quantum Block Image Representation (QBIR), Fourier-based Threshold Quantum Representation (FTQR) and Flexible Representation for Quantum Color Images (FRQCI) — are compared within one variational QNN framework. The main protocol runs the four encodings under a ring-entangled ansatz from 2×2 to 8×8; an ablation repeats the comparison with a hardware-efficient two-design ansatz and a strongly entangling ansatz, at all four resolutions on both datasets. Resource cost is measured as circuit depth, gate count and qubit count, and trainability through per-epoch gradient variance, L2 gradient norm, mean signed gradient and parameter-change magnitude. Every result is a mean ± σ over 20 random seeds.

HCQNN was the strongest overall, with test accuracy up to 0.9756 ± 0.0076 (2×2, noiseless, two-design). Among the fully quantum models, QBIR gave the best balance of accuracy, noise robustness and depth: 0.9396 ± 0.0140 (2×2, noiseless, two-design), and the strongest fully quantum encoding at every resolution under Heron r3 noise. NASS was competitive at low resolution (up to 0.8928 ± 0.0196) but fell to 0.691 at 4×4 under the ring protocol. FTQR and FRQCI did not converge reliably, with test accuracy near chance (≈ 0.50–0.61), consistent with barren plateaus. At 16×16, QBIR needs depth 5,612, 9,701 gates and 16 qubits; FRQCI needs depth 125,299, 164,353 gates and 11 qubits.
Published in The Journal of Supercomputing 82(8):495 (2026).

projects.paper: Quantum image representation-based quantum neural networks for binary classification
layman: A quantum computer cannot look at a picture directly: every pixel first has to be written into a quantum state, and there are many ways to do that. This study compared four of these quantum image encodings (NASS, QBIR, FTQR and FRQCI) to see which ones let a quantum neural network learn well.

Each encoding was placed in the same quantum neural network and trained on the same small images, from 2×2 pixels upwards, many times over with different random starting points. Besides accuracy, the study measured how large the resulting circuits are and whether training gets stuck.

The headline is that the encoding matters a great deal. Among the fully quantum models, QBIR gave the best balance of accuracy, noise robustness and circuit size, while FTQR and FRQCI stayed close to chance, a sign of barren plateaus, where the training signal fades away.

pipeline.stage: Four encodings in one QNN framework

projects.name: Linear-Optical QKD Network Testbeds
projects.blurb: DPS, COW, Twin-Field and MDI QKD simulated over realistic photonic channels with attack modelling.
projects.abstract: Simulation testbeds for differential-phase-shift (DPS), coherent-one-way (COW), twin-field (TF) and measurement-device-independent (MDI) QKD protocols on linear-optical setups in OptiSystem and ANSYS, including loss, noise, and photonic channel impairments. Intercept-resend and photon-number-splitting attacks are modelled, and resource-state and entanglement generation benchmarked.
projects.role: Protocol simulation and attack modelling in Dr. Arpita Maitra's group at TCG CREST, first as a research intern and then as a DRDO Junior Research Fellow.

sections.p: QKD protocols are usually analysed under idealised channel assumptions. Deployment behaviour depends on loss, detector noise, and attacker models that idealised analysis omits.

I built simulation testbeds for four protocols — differential-phase-shift (DPS), coherent-one-way (COW), Twin-Field (TF) and measurement-device-independent (MDI) QKD — in OptiSystem and ANSYS, including loss, noise, and photonic channel impairments.
I modelled intercept-resend and photon-number-splitting attacks and benchmarked resource-state and entanglement generation.
Manuscripts in preparation.

layman: Quantum key distribution (QKD) lets two parties build a shared secret key from single photons; an eavesdropper who interferes leaves traces that can be detected. Textbook analyses usually assume ideal fibres and detectors.
This work built simulated testbeds for four QKD protocols (DPS, COW, Twin-Field and MDI) in optical-design software, with the losses, noise and imperfections of real photonic channels included.

On top of the channels, two classic attacks were modelled: intercept-resend, where the attacker measures and re-sends each photon, and photon-number splitting, where the attacker siphons off extra photons from pulses that carry more than one.

pipeline.stage: DPS, COW, TF and MDI protocol simulation

projects.name: Quantum Circuits for Block Ciphers
projects.blurb: Mini-AES / S-AES circuits with a Grover-based plaintext–ciphertext attack demonstration.
projects.abstract: Quantum circuit designs for an 8-bit AES (Mini-AES / S-AES) with Galois-field arithmetic, run on Qiskit and IBM Quantum hardware, demonstrating Grover key search on a scaled-down cipher, which needs O(√N) oracle queries versus O(N) classically.
projects.role: Research intern — circuit design and attack demonstration.

sections.p: Understanding how symmetric ciphers degrade under quantum attack requires explicit, runnable circuit constructions, not just asymptotic arguments.
I built quantum circuits for an 8-bit AES (Mini-AES / S-AES), including the Galois-field arithmetic the S-box depends on, and ran them on Qiskit and IBM Quantum hardware.

I implemented a plaintext–ciphertext attack with Grover search and amplitude amplification, demonstrating Grover key search on a scaled-down cipher, which needs O(√N) oracle queries versus O(N) classically.
Manuscript in preparation.

layman: Ciphers such as AES scramble data with a secret key. Grover's quantum search could find that key in roughly the square root of the number of guesses a classical brute-force search needs, which is why key lengths matter for a quantum future.

To make this concrete, this project built the full quantum circuit for a miniature 8-bit version of AES, including the finite-field arithmetic inside its S-box, and ran it with Qiskit and on IBM Quantum hardware.
It then used Grover search to recover the key from a known plaintext and ciphertext pair on the scaled-down cipher: a hands-on demonstration of the square-root speed-up.

projects.name: Entanglement Detection via Neural Networks (NMR)
projects.blurb: An ANN that detects genuine multipartite entanglement and assigns SLOCC classes on a three-qubit NMR processor, with the canonical form reducing 128 real features to 18.
projects.abstract: An artificial neural network that detects genuine multipartite entanglement and assigns one of six SLOCC classes to three-qubit states. Each density matrix gives 128 real features (Re and Im of the 64 elements of ρ); the canonical form reduces them to 18 (14 Re, 4 Im), which are then ranked by ANOVA. Validated on 30 experimental pseudopure states from an NMR quantum processor. Published in Quantum Information Processing 24(3), 74 (2025).
projects.role: I worked on the machine-learning side of this study. I explored multiple ANN architectures and configurations, problem formulations, input representations and encodings (one-hot, binary and categorical), and came up with the feature-reduction approach: writing states in canonical form, then ranking the remaining density-matrix elements by ANOVA. V. Gulati handled the experimental side: sample preparation, NMR gate preparation, the physical experiments and measurements, and the analysis and cleaning of the raw experimental data.

sections.p: Detecting genuine multipartite entanglement in experimental NMR systems is hard: witnesses are state-specific and full state tomography is experimentally costly. The trained model needs only a few elements (4 for GME, 6 for SLOCC), which points to reduced-measurement protocols; here they were read off reconstructed states.

An ANN detects genuine multipartite entanglement and assigns one of six SLOCC classes. Each state gives 128 real features (Re and Im of the 64 elements of ρ); writing states in canonical form leaves 18 (14 Re, 4 Im), which are then ranked by ANOVA. The model is trained on simulated states (12 × 10³ states) and tested on 30 experimental three-qubit states prepared on an NMR quantum processor.

Validated on 30 experimental three-qubit pseudopure states from an NMR processor: GME detection reached 0.954 ± 0.046 accuracy with 4 features, and SLOCC classification 0.867 ± 0.090 with 6 (overall accuracy over the experimental states, Tables IV–V). The ANN is benchmarked against SVM and KNN, and against existing three-qubit classification schemes (the 3-tangle and correlation tensors).
Published in Quantum Information Processing 24(3), 74 (2025); preprint arXiv:2409.19739.

projects.paper: ANN-enhanced detection of multipartite entanglement in a three-qubit NMR quantum processor
layman: Entanglement is the quantum link that lets particles share correlations no classical system can. Three qubits can be entangled in different ways, and telling these kinds apart in a real experiment usually means reconstructing the full quantum state, which is costly.

This study trained a neural network to do the sorting. Given the numbers that describe a three-qubit state, it says whether the state is genuinely entangled across all three qubits, and which of six entanglement classes it belongs to.

A key step was shrinking the input. A full description has 128 numbers; writing states in a standard (canonical) form leaves 18, and the trained network needs only a handful of those: 4 for the entanglement test and 6 for the classes. Trained on simulated states, it was tested on 30 states prepared on a real NMR quantum processor.

projects.name: VQLS for Financial Time-Series Forecasting
projects.blurb: A variational quantum linear solver applied end to end to next-day stock price forecasting on real market data.
projects.abstract: A variational quantum linear solver (VQLS) applied to time series forecasting on real financial market data. Hankel-like trajectory matrices are built from historical Reliance Industries stock prices and the resulting linear system is solved with a quantum-classical hybrid approach: Hadamard test circuits evaluate the cost function, COBYLA optimizes the variational parameters, and a SWAP test estimates the overlap of the solution state with recent market data to give the next-day forecast. Quantum advantage is not realized at this problem scale (2 × 2 system), and classical baselines reach equivalent accuracy; the workflow runs end to end on the Aer simulator with shallow circuits (depth ~6) compatible with NISQ hardware, and the paper identifies its scalability bottlenecks.

sections.p: Existing VQLS demonstrations focus on synthetic test cases; practical deployment on domain-specific data remains sparse. The question was whether the quantum-classical hybrid architecture can be validated on an authentic forecasting workflow before hardware scales.

A Hankel-like trajectory matrix is built from daily closing prices of Reliance Industries (January to April 2023) and decomposed into a Pauli basis. Hadamard test circuits evaluate the VQLS cost function, COBYLA optimizes the variational parameter with 10,000 shots per circuit, and a SWAP test estimates the overlap of the solution state with recent market data to give the next-day forecast. All circuits run in Qiskit on the Aer simulator.

The workflow runs end to end on the Aer simulator with shallow circuits (depth ~6) compatible with NISQ hardware, and the solution is verified against AR(1) and linear regression baselines. Quantum advantage is not realized at this 2 × 2 scale, and the classical baselines reach equivalent accuracy in negligible time. The paper identifies the scalability bottlenecks: exponential growth of the Pauli decomposition and COBYLA shot overhead.
Published by IEEE, 2026.

projects.paper: Variational Quantum Linear Solver for Time Series Forecasting: A Practical Implementation on Financial Data
layman: Many forecasting methods come down to solving a system of linear equations. The variational quantum linear solver (VQLS) is a near-term quantum algorithm for exactly that, but it has mostly been shown on made-up test problems.

This project ran VQLS end to end on real data. Daily closing prices of Reliance Industries from January to April 2023 were turned into a small (2 × 2) linear system, solved with quantum circuits on a simulator, and the result was used to forecast the next day's price.

It is an honest test: at this tiny size there is no quantum advantage, and simple classical methods are just as accurate and much faster. The value is in running the whole workflow and showing exactly where it would have to scale.

projects.name: TensNet: Tensor Networks for 2D Flow Simulation
projects.blurb: A tensor network library using MPS and MPO for memory-efficient simulation of 2D incompressible flow.
projects.abstract: TensNet is a library implementing tensor network methods, using Matrix Product States (MPS) and Matrix Product Operators (MPO), for simulating the 2D incompressible Navier–Stokes equations. It is designed to reduce memory use compared with standard grid-based solvers, keeping accuracy through adaptive bond-dimension truncation; it uses the DMRG algorithm to solve the implicit pressure-correction equations and cross-approximation to handle complex immersed boundaries.

sections.p: Computational fluid dynamics simulations demand enormous memory for storing high-resolution velocity fields, which is a barrier to practical simulations on resource-constrained systems.

TensNet represents flow fields as Matrix Product States and operators as Matrix Product Operators, compressing them by SVD truncation with adaptive bond dimensions. The two-site DMRG algorithm solves the implicit Poisson equations in the pressure-correction scheme, and cross-approximation represents immersed boundaries and obstacle geometries as MPS. Benchmarks: a cylinder in cross-flow, a square obstacle and a 3×2 array of cylinders, compared against a dense finite-difference solution on the same grid.

p: Reported in the submitted manuscript (under review at ICSSCC 2026).
Setup: Intel i7 workstation with 16 GB RAM and no GPU; 256 × 64 grid, Δt = 10⁻³, ν = 0.01; accuracy measured against a dense finite-difference solution on the same grid.

At D_max = 30 the L2 error is below 10⁻² and memory falls from about 8 GB to 5.8 MB, a reduction of roughly 1.4 × 10³. The L2 velocity error falls roughly exponentially with D_max at Re = 15, 30, 100 and 500; higher Re needs a moderately larger D_max.
Scalability: on a 1024 × 256 grid with D_max = 50, TensNet uses about 35 MB; the manuscript estimates about 2 TB for a dense finite-difference solver.

projects.paper: TensNet: Memory-Efficient Tensor Network Methods for 2D Incompressible Flow Simulation
projects.role: TensNet was originally developed by N. Khan and S. S. Pandey. I carried out the testing, code troubleshooting, benchmarking and visualisation, and prepared the manuscript.
layman: Simulating how a fluid flows, for example air around a pillar, means storing the velocity at every point of a fine grid, which quickly needs gigabytes of memory.

TensNet stores those flow fields in a compressed form borrowed from quantum physics: tensor networks, specifically matrix product states. One setting, the bond dimension, controls how much detail is kept; larger means more accurate and more memory.
In the submitted manuscript, the compressed simulations stay close to a standard full-grid solver while using megabytes instead of gigabytes on the test cases.

projects.name: Bitter Solenoid Simulator (0.5 T)
projects.blurb: A real-time simulator for a 0.5 T water-cooled copper Bitter solenoid, with Swiss-roll RF metamaterials for early-stage fMRI.
projects.abstract: An open-source simulator that couples the field, electrical, thermal, hydraulic and mechanical models of a 0.5 T water-cooled copper Bitter solenoid, optimises the design under engineering constraints, and adds an fMRI layer: shim coils, B0 stability and an RF signal-to-noise model with Swiss-roll metamaterials. It runs on a laptop, Kaggle or Colab, and a browser demo needs no install.

sections.p: Design a 0.5 T water-cooled copper Bitter solenoid for early-stage fMRI and evaluate it in real time on modest hardware (a 32 GB Ryzen 5 laptop, Kaggle or Colab), using only Python-3.6-compatible NumPy, SciPy, Numba and Matplotlib APIs that existed before July 2018.

The continuum simulator couples closed-form and exact elliptic-integral field models (checked against an independent straight-segment Biot–Savart engine), Bitter-plate electrics, thermal and hydraulic models of the axial cooling holes (Dittus–Boelter, with a Gnielinski check) and Lorentz-force mechanics. Differential evolution followed by SLSQP minimises electrical plus pump power subject to 0.5 T at the centre, a copper hot spot of at most 85 °C, a supply of at most 8 V, an inner radius of at least 50 mm, at most 100 ppm inhomogeneity, a pressure drop of at most 5 bar and Re ≥ 10⁴. A separate fMRI layer adds Z2/Z4 shim loops, B0 stability and a quasi-static RF SNR model of Swiss-roll metamaterials. A mesoscopic emulation layer adds tolerance and contact-resistance scatter, and particle estimators re-derive the continuum numbers as a cross-check.

p: From the repository's generated results (differential-evolution run, seed 1).

The optimum has an inner radius of 50.0 mm, an outer radius of 300 mm and a 1.10 m stack. It carries 2576 A at 4.54 V, dissipating 11.7 kW plus 81 W of pump power, with 99.95 ppm peak-to-peak homogeneity over a 30 mm-diameter sphere and a 25.9 °C copper hot spot. The active limits are field homogeneity and size, not cooling.
Two Z2/Z4 shim-loop pairs bring the homogeneity over the same sphere to 0.26 ppm.
In the quasi-static RF model, a Swiss-roll slab improves SNR over the same coil held off over an air gap, but does not beat a coil placed directly on the tissue.

projects.name: Sexually Antagonistic Selection
projects.blurb: 2019 project on sexually antagonistic selection in Dr. N. G. Prasad's Evolutionary Biology Lab (EBL), IISER Mohali.
projects.abstract: A 2019 project on sexually antagonistic selection in the Evolutionary Biology Lab of Dr. N. G. Prasad at IISER Mohali, with a public repository of computational models of sexual conflict in Drosophila.

sections.p: A 2019 project on sexually antagonistic selection in the Evolutionary Biology Lab (EBL) of Dr. N. G. Prasad, IISER Mohali.

The public repository rebuilds published models of sexual conflict: a two-locus model for the resolution of intra-locus sexual conflict from a poster by the lab, Parsons' (1961) invasion conditions with Owen's (1953) equilibria, and a "mother's curse" cytonuclear model. Each is solved twice: as deterministic recursions, and as an individual-based simulation that never imports the analytical maths. Statistical tests then check whether the simulated populations reproduce each prediction. A second part models published sexual-antagonism results from the lab with a hybrid analytic, individual-based and emulator approach.

publications.authors: A. Tiwari, S. Kumar, P. Tyagi, S. Siyanwal, S. Sakhuja
publications.abstract: We apply five quantum machine learning models (QGRU, QLSTM, QNN, VQC and QSVM) to meteorological time-series data from the ERA5 reanalysis dataset, for both regression (forecasting) and classification tasks.

sections.p: Whether current QML models can be used for weather prediction, and where hardware limits and noise constrain them.

Meteorological features from ERA5 single-level data for Safdarjung, Delhi, are preprocessed and fed to quantum recurrent (QGRU, QLSTM), variational (VQC, QNN) and kernel (QSVM) models. Each model is evaluated on regression and classification tasks, and compared with classical baselines: LSTM and SVM (built by me) and GRU and ANN (built by S. Sakhuja).
The models reach reasonable accuracy on both prediction and classification, best on binary classification. Hardware limitations and noise limit scalability and generalisation.

publications.role: I built the QLSTM and QSVM models and their classical baselines (LSTM and SVM), extracted the dataset from ERA5, and carried out the data analysis. S. Sakhuja carried out the remaining work.

publications.title: Quantum image representation-based quantum neural networks for binary classification
publications.authors: A. Tiwari*, S. Siyanwal*, S. Sakhuja, S. Kumar, P. Tyagi
publications.abstract: A controlled comparison of four quantum image representations (NASS, QBIR, FTQR, FRQCI) inside one variational quantum neural network framework for image classification on near-term (NISQ) devices, tested on binary MNIST (0 vs 1) and a three-class FashionMNIST subset at resolutions from 2×2 to 16×16, under both noiseless simulation and a calibrated noise model of the IBM Heron r3 processor. Two reference models, a quanvolutional network (QCNN) and a hybrid CNN–QNN (HCQNN), place the encodings against established baselines.
publications.note: NASS, QBIR, FTQR, FRQCI; binary MNIST 0/1 at 2×2 to 16×16; three-class FashionMNIST.

publications.title: ANN-enhanced detection of multipartite entanglement in a three-qubit NMR quantum processor
publications.authors: V. Gulati*, S. Siyanwal*, Arvind, K. Dorai
publications.abstract: An artificial neural network identifies which of the six SLOCC classes an experimentally generated three-qubit pseudopure state belongs to, and detects genuine multipartite entanglement. The 128 real features (Re and Im of the 64 elements of ρ) are reduced to 18 (14 Re, 4 Im) by the canonical form, then ranked by ANOVA; the model is trained on simulated states, validated on 30 experimental states from an NMR quantum processor, and benchmarked against SVM and KNN.
publications.note: Grew out of the BS–MS thesis at IISER Mohali (advisor Prof. Kavita Dorai).

publications.title: Entanglement detection and gate optimization in the system of three and four NMR qubits using deep learning and machine learning
publications.status: held in the IISER Mohali library; not yet public (to be released with the supervisor's permission)
publications.abstract: This thesis applies machine learning and deep learning to two tasks in NMR quantum computing. The first is detecting and classifying entanglement in two-, three- and four-qubit states. The second is optimizing quantum gates by designing radio-frequency pulse sequences with a genetic algorithm.
publications.note: BS–MS thesis. Supervisor: Prof. Kavita Dorai.
related: ANN-enhanced detection of multipartite entanglement in a three-qubit NMR quantum processor

sections.p: Entanglement witnesses detect only some entangled states. Full state tomography detects them all, but the number of measurements it needs grows exponentially with system size. Separately, implementing high-fidelity gates on NMR hardware requires breaking each gate into an optimized sequence of pulses.

p: Neural networks (Keras/TensorFlow) trained on simulated pure-state density matrices: 15,000 states (2 qubits), 100,000 (3 qubits) and 70,000 (4 qubits). Labels were entangled vs separable for 2 qubits, and separability classes for 3 and 4 qubits.

K-nearest neighbours and PCA + K-means on 50,000, 100,000 and 70,000 simulated pure states; PCA + K-means was also applied to 54 experimental two-qubit NMR states provided by V. Gulati, and their theoretical counterparts. A GAN with a complex-valued pseudo-siamese network was used for two-qubit states.

Gate optimization: a genetic algorithm, following the approach of Devra et al., that searches over sequences of hard pulses and delays (pulse width, phase and delay), using gate fidelity as the fitness function.

Neural networks: validation accuracy of 0.9997 (2 qubits), 0.9971 (3) and 0.9996 (4) on simulated pure states. They could not separate states within the fully entangled class, such as GHZ and W states.
K-nearest neighbours: best accuracy of 0.9981 (2 qubits, k = 3), 0.9862 (3 qubits, k = 1 or 3) and 0.9619 (4 qubits, k = 15 or 17).

PCA + K-means formed cluster boundaries for 2-, 3- and 4-qubit states; how accurate those boundaries are was left for further study. The GAN + pseudo-siamese network, trained only on separable two-qubit states, classified entangled states in the test set.

Genetic-algorithm pulse design: for a two-qubit homonuclear system, the thesis reports a gate fidelity of 0.8513 (about 8 hours of computation). It was not fully optimized and was not tested on the NMR hardware.
Open problems identified: training on noisy states, and working from incomplete tomography. The three-qubit classification on experimental NMR data was developed further into the published paper.

statement: My work connects quantum information research with production engineering: what it takes to run a quantum algorithm on hardware under real constraints (noise, latency, memory bandwidth) and keep it working reliably.

That has led me across three connected areas. In variational quantum algorithms and quantum machine learning, I study how data encoding and circuit structure affect resource cost (circuit depth, gate count, qubits) and how hybrid pipelines perform on real forecasting tasks. In quantum hardware acceleration, I co-authored work (first author N. Khan) that compiles trained variational circuits into state-vector simulation kernels on FPGA fabric for low-latency inference. In photonic quantum networks, I simulate QKD protocols over lossy channels and model intercept-resend and photon-number-splitting attacks.

My MS research at IISER Mohali used neural networks to detect genuine multipartite entanglement and classify SLOCC classes on a three-qubit NMR processor (co-first author, Quantum Information Processing, 2025).
I think quantum research moves faster when its artefacts are built like software: tested, versioned, reproducible and deployable.
